entries.title: Pennsylvania Democrats Pile on Fetterman While Senators Stay Silent
entries.summary: A party swap by Fetterman could put any hope of a Senate Democratic majority in jeopardy — leaving his colleagues in a bind over whether to speak out against him.
entries.content:
Pennsylvania Democrats lashed out at Sen. John Fetterman following his surprise video appearance at the Republican midterm convention on Wednesday night, with Rep. Chris Deluzio saying Republicans can “have him.”

But even as the party struggles with whether to denounce Fetterman for the move, his counterparts in the Senate have, by and large, remained quiet.

Senate Democrats are looking to flip four seats in the upper chamber with just weeks to go until the November midterms — and a party swap by the Pennsylvania Democrat would likely put that effort in jeopardy.

One Democratic operative who works with Democratic lawmakers said that senators are likely concerned that publicly criticizing their colleague could only push him away.

“You can’t go around yelling at your coworkers if you have to turn around and do something with them,” the operative said. “That is literally the work of looking toward a governing majority or minority, depending on how this all shakes out in November.”

Another campaign operative granted anonymity to speak candidly told The Washington Sun that he would advise Democrats to start building a “Fetterman-proof majority.”

“If I was a Senate Democrat, I would do anything to flip five seats instead of four,” the operative said. “I would do anything to make sure we can have a Fetterman-proof majority.”

Fetterman said in a statement to The Sun shortly after his video appearance that he had no plans to switch parties, saying “should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on.”

But his participation in the GOP convention follows months of speculation that he could be considering a move to the other side. The senator, who was endorsed by progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) during his 2023 run for office, has increasingly voted with Republicans on issues like government funding and the Iran war this year and has more frequently voiced his disdain for the left wing of the party.

“I’m always going to stand with America. I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life,” Fetterman said in his videoed convention appearance.

His appearance also followed reporting in The Wall Street Journal last week that his frustration with the party has been mounting. Fetterman has become exasperated with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and once wrote “I truly don’t care” when aides informed him that Schumer was organizing a special conference call for Democrats, according to the Journal report.

Schumer urged Fetterman to stay in the Democratic caucus while speaking to reporters in July, praising him as a “very good” member of Congress. His comments came after Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Republicans would “welcome” Fetterman into their conference, adding that he’s had “conversations” with the maverick senator about making the switch.

“The people in our caucus very much like him and respect him, and we’re a big tent party. We can have a lot of different views in that party,” Schumer said.

But even as senators — like Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vermont), who told Politico “it’s a waste of energy to get spun up” about Fetterman — refuse to dump on their colleague, Pennsylvania Democrats have piled criticism on the senator.

Rep. Brendan Boyle, who is reportedly mulling a challenge for Fetterman’s seat in 2028, said in an interview with MSNow on Thursday that he “hopes and prays” Fetterman will stay true to his word and remain a member of the Senate Democratic Caucus, but stands by his comments calling him a “disgrace.”

“Obviously, there are all sorts of concerns about Senator Fetterman. I think that’s probably going to continue,” Boyle said. “He has always been, throughout his career, a guy who will do the performative stuff. The things that will get him the most attention.”

And Rep. Madeleine Dean, another Pennsylvania Democrat, also expressed concern about Fetterman’s convention appearance. At a Democratic counterprogramming event in Dallas, Dean said she was “disappointed” by Fetterman’s “stunt.”

“We can see in his work ethics that he’s just not present. He doesn’t participate much at all in his own committees, let alone attend them,” she said. “From the ground, from suburban Philadelphia, my constituents are livid. Those who went out and knocked doors for him — they are absolutely livid.”

entries.title: Vance Urges Hesitant Voters to Shelve Concerns Over Iran War
entries.summary: The vice president asked Republicans not to “throw out the baby with the bath water” if they disagree with the administration’s foreign policy.
entries.content:
Vice President JD Vance urged voters uneasy with the Iran war to stick with Republicans for the midterms, acknowledging the conflict’s unpopularity among Americans as it stretches past six months.

The vice president’s appeal to Republicans on day two of the party’s midterm convention in Dallas marked a crucial point in the administration’s recognition of how unpopular some of their policies are among members of their base ahead of November.

Vance said he was speaking directly to voters on the fence and people “who love some of our policies but maybe don’t agree with others.” Referencing the late conservative commentator Charlie Kirk, who died a year ago on Sept. 10, the vice president asked voters to coalesce around Republicans, even if they disagree with the White House’s actions.

“Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater. Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there,” Vance said on Thursday.

“I’m not asking anybody to agree with me on every single policy of the administration,” the vice president added. “What I am asking you to do is to recognize the contrast with the radicals and recognize the achievements of the last 18 months.”

In his 40-minute speech, Vance didn’t express opposition to the war, which is widely unpopular: Roughly two-thirds of Americans — and an even greater percentage of young voters — oppose the conflict, according to a July poll from The Associated Press.

Vance briefly mentioned young men throughout his speech, also while referencing Kirk. Some young men have said they are disillusioned by the president’s second term, with Trump’s approval rating among the group sinking by about 10 percentage points earlier this year.

Trump downplayed those concerns when Fox News’ Laura Ingraham asked about “demoralized” young male supporters during an interview that aired earlier Thursday evening.

“I don’t think they’re demoralized — I think they’re very proud of the fact that I’m not letting Iran have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said. “I disagree with you.”

In between hammering Democrats on affordability and promising additional economic boosts should Republicans maintain congressional control, Vance also spoke at length Thursday about Americans’ “birthright” ownership over the country. He cited an inaccurate figure of 25 million immigrants allowed through the border under the Biden administration and cast undocumented immigrants as responsible for employment and housing shortages. The vice president said Americans had grown tired of factory closures, overdoses and rising costs.

“We were tired of being called racist for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous,” he said.

When a protester interrupted waving a flag, Vance derided the person’s prop as anti-American for several minutes, prompting long cheers from the audience.

“Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket,” he said, firing up the arena’s crowd, which chanted “48! 48!” in a reference to a potential future Vance presidency.

The vice president also spent a portion of his remarks mocking Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed — who recently quipped that second lady Usha Vance would not have met her grandfather-in-law because of her race — and Texas Senate nominee James Talarico.

He jabbed at Talarico’s past comments about gender, including God being “non-binary” — remarks the candidate has since walked back.

“I don’t know about you,” Vance said, ”but I never want to see that guy’s web browser history.”

entries.title: Trump Returns to Affordability Messaging as Voters’ Economic Attitudes Sour
entries.summary: The president also doubled down on his desire to send $5,000 checks to American adults, even as some members of his own party question how the proposal would work.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump on Thursday reiterated his promise to distribute $5,000 checks if Republicans retain control of Congress in November, disregarding growing concerns over the proposal in favor of energizing the base on promises to improve affordability.

Trump’s remarks on the second day of the party’s midterm convention in Dallas were shorter and more toned down than his announcement the day before: The president focused on affordability with promises to make permanent his policies cutting certain taxes and prescription drug pricing.

“That alone should get us a big victory in our midterms that are coming up,” Trump said of his prescription drug policies. “Get out and vote, please.”

Trump and Vice President JD Vance’s choice to highlight the economy Thursday evening — without acknowledging recent fallout from the nation’s mounting trade war with Canada or record-high oil prices from the Iran war — reflects voters’ top issue in the final months before the midterms. A growing share of Americans say the administration’s economic policies have worsened conditions in the country, according to a July Pew Research survey.

Trump unveiled his idea to distribute dividends on Wednesday night, telling the crowd that if Republicans win both the House and Senate, “you win with us and you get $5,000.”

The proposition — one of many promises the president has made throughout his tenure to distribute cash or checks directly to Americans — would probably cost over $1.2 trillion and could balloon the federal debt. Trump has not laid out a detailed proposal for how to pay for the dividends, though he suggested tariffs could help fund them while speaking to Fox News’ Laura Ingraham in an interview that aired Thursday evening.

Key Republicans say they were blindsided by Trump’s pledge, noting that the White House did not consult beforehand with GOP congressional leadership, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune. The president told Ingraham he has spoken to Thune and House Speaker Mike Johnson, despite also telling CBS News on Thursday that he doesn’t need the Hill’s approval to go through with the payments.

“I do speak to them. We can do it,” Trump said on Fox News.

“A lot of people think I don’t even need congressional approval because we have made so much money,” he added, saying the country has financially benefited from fees associated with companies such as TikTok and Intel. “I see that some people are saying, ‘That’s communism.’ It’s not communism — it’s actually good entrepreneurship.”

Thune’s and Johnson’s offices did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Democrats and Republicans have largely rebuked the proposition as costly and potentially illegal.

Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) called the decision “flat out illegal,” citing a federal law that prohibits offering payments in exchange for voting behavior, while Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom of California accused Trump of trying to “buy your vote.”

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, said the plan would lead to more debt and inflation.

“What I don’t think you want to do is borrow another $1.5 trillion, and then just try to flood that into the economy, because that will lead to more inflation,” DeSantis said at a press conference in Miami on Thursday. He suggested that instead, the president should “cut people’s tax and return it to the people.”

Some elected officials publicly embraced the idea, including Vance, who said on Wednesday that the plan would help Americans share some of the country’s “incredible wealth” — though he did not mention the checks during his Thursday night convention speech.

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said in a social media post that he “will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election.”

A campaign text sent to Texas voters Thursday afternoon contained an abbreviated link with an “attachment” for the $5,000 check it said the president “just authorized.” The URL redirects to the WinRed fundraising page for Eric Flores, a Texas Republican running for a U.S. House seat.

Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat running for governor, said in a statement that she supports the idea to send $5,000 to Texans, but “it can’t be about who’s in power — it has to be about giving the people their power back.” She promised that, if elected, she would deliver “$1,500 Corruption Tax Refund checks” to help working families who faced “the cost of [Gov.] Greg Abbott’s corruption.”
entries.author: Torrie Herrington
